name: Lesotho
sources: GDP $0.6bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series LSO, 1990 = 596,410,264, on real growth of +6.05%. THE SMALLEST ECONOMY IN THIS ROSTER. And the figure is misleading in a way that has to be stated rather than left for the model to trip over: Lesotho's GDP and its national income are different quantities by a larger margin than anywhere else on this board. GDP is $330 a head; GNI per capita on the World Bank Atlas basis for 1990 is $510 (NY.GNP.PCAP.CD, series LSO, 1990 = 510), because roughly 120,000 Basotho men — a very large share of the adult male workforce — were down South African gold mines and sending the money home. Migrant remittances ran at something like 40% of GNP. The model holds output produced inside the border and therefore cannot see the half of Lesotho's income that was earned in the Free State and the Transvaal.
Population 1.8m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series LSO, 1990 = 1,809,696.

TFP trend 0.004: set level with Kenya and Zimbabwe. There is very little to be productive with — 10% of Lesotho is arable, the highlands are grazing, and the manufacturing sector was a handful of relocated Taiwanese and South African garment plants using Lesotho as a way around sanctions. What was under construction was the one real asset: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, agreed with South Africa by treaty on 24 October 1986, which would sell Orange river water to Gauteng and give Lesotho its only significant export that was not a person.

Inflation 11.6%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series LSO, 1990 = 11.63. It tracks South Africa's closely and it must: the loti was pegged one-for-one to the rand under the Common Monetary Area and the rand circulated as legal tender inside Lesotho. Lesotho had no independent monetary policy in 1990 and the model should be read as pricing the rand.

Interest rate 20.4%: World Bank FR.INR.LEND, series LSO, 1990 = 20.42, a genuine 1990 print. Against 11.6% inflation that is a real rate near +9 points, which is not a Central Bank of Lesotho decision but a South African one transmitted through the peg. The loader's coupled check reads 0.025 - (0.2042 - 0.1163) = -0.063.

Revenue 37% of GDP: INTERPOLATED AND FLAGGED. World Bank GC.REV.XGRT.GD.ZS, series LSO, has no 1990 entry; it prints 40.41 for 1989 and 34.47 for 1991, and 0.37 is the midpoint of the two bracketing years. It is high for a country this poor for one reason: the Southern African Customs Union revenue pool, which paid Lesotho a share of the common external tariff far above what its own trade generated and was the single largest line in the budget.

Military 3.6% of GDP: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS, series LSO, 1990 = 3.55. A high burden on a tiny base, and it buys a force that could not defend the country against anything — which is the correct reading. What Lesotho's security spending was actually for was internal: the Royal Lesotho Defence Force was the instrument of the coup of 20 January 1986 and of every subsequent change of government.

Investment 24% of GDP, split 15 state / 9 private: NOT SOURCED. NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS has no Lesotho entry for 1990, so both figures are brackets and are flagged. The total is set high for a country this poor and weighted toward the state because Phase 1A of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project — the Katse dam and the transfer tunnel — was under way from 1988 and was, relative to the size of the economy, one of the largest construction projects any country has ever attempted.
Debt 41% of GDP: World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS, series LSO, 1990 = 41.32, external debt stocks as a share of GNI. Moderate, concessional, and about to rise with the Highlands project.

Oil 0.0: no production and no refinery. Every litre came in by road from South Africa, which is what the border blockade of 1 January 1986 demonstrated — Pretoria closed the crossings over ANC sanctuary, Lesotho ran out of fuel and food within three weeks, and the army removed the government on 20 January.

Stability 45 and authoritarianism 0.80: Lesotho in January 1990 was governed by a Military Council under Major General Justin Metsing Lekhanya, with no parliament, no legal political activity and no election since 1970 — the last election Lesotho held, in 1970, was annulled by the Basotho National Party when it lost. Authoritarianism 0.80 is a junta and is set below Malawi's 0.85 because Lekhanya's council was neither ideological nor especially capable of controlling the country. Stability 45 is level with Zambia's and is generous only if the reader stops at January: Lekhanya stripped King Moshoeshoe II of his executive powers in February 1990, the King went into exile in March, was deposed in November and replaced by his son Letsie III, and Lekhanya himself was overthrown by Colonel Elias Ramaema on 30 April 1991. NONE OF THAT IS ENCODED. The number is the position on the start date and the sim can do what it likes with it.

Separatism 0.02: none, and Lesotho is the reason the field can go this low. It is one of the very few states in Africa that is a nation — one people, one language, one historic kingdom assembled by Moshoeshoe I in the 1820s, with borders that enclose all of it. The territorial grievance runs outward rather than inward and is discussed in the roster row in nations.rs, where it is deliberately not entered as a claim.

Military strength 0.5: THE LOWEST INDEX IN THIS ROSTER, below Bahrain's 0.6. The Royal Lesotho Defence Force was about 2,000 men, effectively a paramilitary gendarmerie with a couple of light aircraft, and its entire operational history is coups against its own government. Against South Africa, the only state it borders, it is a rounding error, and that ratio — an army of two thousand entirely surrounded by an army of a hundred thousand with nuclear weapons — is the fact the dyad model most needs to be able to see.
